Michael — thanks for the run-through last week. Procurement asked for a conservative mapping from our expected token profile to an initial committed slab so they can start approvals. 2) We also need a recommended headroom percentage for the first 3 months (conservative preferred).

Appreciate it — Jordan

Subject: Re: Estimating committed capacity — quick data + ask

Jordan — thanks, got the CSV. Kim/ Priya are looping in the sensitivity simulator and a few assumptions below so procurement has numbers. High level summary up front: with your peak token mix and a 200ms p95 SLO, an H100-80 slab (dedicated pool of 8x H100 cards) gives the most predictable headroom for the first 3 months; an A100-80 slab can be cheaper but hits SLO tail under bursty 95th percentile requests unless you accept larger headroom.

Key assumptions (we used the attached spreadsheet):
- Model: open-7B-quant (q4_0 equivalent) — similar compute per token to mid-sized causal models
- Avg tokens per request: 1,200; p95 request tokens: 9,000; peak concurrent requests modeled from 60k tokens/day concentrated in 1-hour peak window.
- Baseline throughput: H100-80 single slab (8 GPUs) continuous: ~2,200 tokens/sec sustained (single-user aggregate across pool) at 30ms per-token kernel latency; A100-80: ~1,450 tokens/sec sustained given same workload and batcher config.
- Latency mapping: we modeled end-to-end p95 = kernel latency + batching latency + network (assume 12ms). Batching increases with load; we kept target batch latency <= 80ms to meet 200ms p95 goal.

Short table (simulator outputs):
- A100-80 single slab (8x80GB): site sustained throughput ~1,450 tok/s; at 200ms p95, safe committed TPS = 700 tok/s (50% headroom recommendation)
- H100-80 single slab (8x80GB): sustained ~2,200 tok/s; at 200ms p95, safe committed TPS = 1,320 tok/s (40% headroom)
- H100-80 with burst pool (8 + 2 spare GPUs): sustained ~2,400 tok/s; safe committed TPS = 1,600 tok/s (35% headroom)

Recommendations for month 0-3: start with 1x H100-80 slab + 2-GPU burst reserve (or an H100-80 with burst policy) and commit to a tokens/sec band at ~1,200 tok/s. That keeps you comfortably under p95 200ms during modeled beta peaks and gives room for prompt/usage growth. If budget is tighter, you can choose A100-80 but plan for 70% headroom early (commit lower TPS, route overflow to hosted instances).

I've attached the spreadsheet export (commit_sensitivity_simulator.xlsx) with the scenarios and the exact parameterization. Priya — can you confirm pricing delta for a 3-month reserved slab vs on-demand?

—Michael

Jordan — follow-up on the simulator knobs and an explicit runbook for the first 90 days. I'm pasting the short runbook and a few command-level notes taken from the spreadsheet so your SRE/procurement team can validate quickly.

Runbook (first 90 days):
1) Provision: 1x H100-80 slab in us-east with burst policy (2 GPUs warm standby).
2) Configure: batcher target max-wait = 60ms; max-batch = 64 tokens-per-batch heuristic tuned to avg 1.2k requests.
3) Monitoring: p95 latency alert at 180ms, token usage / sec alert when sustained > 85% of committed TPS for 10m.
4) Auto-fallback: when sustained > committed TPS for 2m -> route overflow to hosted nodes (same model variant) with a 2x cost flag and notify account team.
5) Month-1 review: compare observed p95 and prompt sizes; if avg prompt >1,500 tokens, prepare to increase commit band by 20% or enable additional 1x H100 slab as seasonal buffer.

Sensitivity notes from simulator:
- Prompt growth +25% -> required headroom increases ~15–22% (nonlinear due to batching hit).
- p95 tail heat spikes (10x background short bursts) cause batching latency to dominate; if you expect bursty p95 events, prefer H100 over A100 for lower kernel latency.

I've exported the param tab where you can change: model flops-per-token, effective batch size, network RTT, and it recalculates safe committed TPS and suggested headroom. If you'd like, we can run this against your live telemetry next week and produce an operationalized commit letter for procurement.

—Kim
Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference
